deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated entries.

(A) Lines 1-8 continue the entry begun at the foot of the previous page. That entry reads: 'Mapping of a finite, simply connected n-dimensional region onto another such region so that the mapping functions satisfy n linear partial differential equations. This seems to be the right generalization of conformal mapping. Example for 4-dimensional space is the mapping by ...'. The page opens with '-dung durch f(u,w), f'(u,w)', completing 'Abbildung'.

Modern restatement (interpretation mine): let u, w be complex variables, so (u,w) lies in C^2 = R^4. The map (u,w) -> (f(u,w), f'(u,w)) is given by a pair of holomorphic functions of two complex variables. Write u = x1 + i y1 and w = x2 + i y2. The real and imaginary parts of each component satisfy the Cauchy-Riemann system in each variable separately: dRe/dx_k = dIm/dy_k and dRe/dy_k = -dIm/dx_k for k = 1, 2. This is a linear first-order PDE system, and its solutions are closed under composition, exactly as in the planar case n = 2.

Note on counting: the full Cauchy-Riemann system for two components in two variables is 8 real equations, not literally 'n = 4'. Hilbert's phrase 'n linear PDEs' should therefore be read loosely as 'a system of linear PDEs'. This reading is mine.

Hilbert then poses the structural question: which functions of solutions of the linear system again satisfy the same system? In modern terms, for which linear first-order systems do the solution maps form a pseudogroup (closure under composition and inversion), as conformal maps do in the plane?

He marks n = 3 as the most important case. Implicit motivation (mine): by Liouville's theorem (1850), conformal maps in dimension >= 3 reduce to Moebius transformations, so a richer class is needed in R^3. He suggests the familiar linear PDEs of physics might lead to a solution, citing W. Voigt, 'Elementare Mechanik' (1889), p. 376, and H. Hertz, 'Die Prinzipien der Mechanik' (1894). The Hertz reference dates the entry to about 1894-95, consistent with the 1894 Caen congress cited on the previous page. No derivation is carried out; this is a research programme note.

(B) Lines 9-20 are a methodological parable about ideal theory. Someone wants to get from a lonely island to the opposite pole of the Earth. One way is a finite number of procedures: first build the tools, then a boat, and so on. One reaches the goal provided one lives long enough. The same goal is reached faster and more surely by a single procedure: ordering by telegraph a ticket for the next express steamer, which at the same time makes the whole globe accessible. 'Such an express steamer is the theory of ideals.'

The point is the contrast between step-by-step elimination or computation (finite but impractical) and a conceptual theory (the ideal theory of Dedekind/Kronecker as Hilbert was then developing it for the Zahlbericht and invariant theory). The conceptual route settles the question at once and uniformly for all cases. There is no mathematics to check in (B).
errors: Part (A): the 4-dimensional example via two holomorphic functions of two complex variables is governed by 8 real Cauchy-Riemann equations, so 'n linear PDEs' with n = 4 does not literally fit. This is a loose formulation rather than an error of computation.

Part (A): no proof or precise condition is given; the composition-closure question is posed, not answered. Liouville's rigidity (conformal maps in R^3 are Moebius) shows that the naive conformal generalization to n = 3 is too restrictive. This is presumably why Hilbert seeks other linear systems, but he does not state it.
Part (B): 'durch durch' is a dittography in the manuscript; 'vorausge-[setzt] dass' is split across the line break.

results.what: Proposal: generalize conformal mapping to n dimensions as diffeomorphisms whose components satisfy a linear PDE system closed under composition; example C^2 via pairs of holomorphic functions of two complex variables; emphasis on n = 3 and on PDEs of physics
results.modern_name: Pseudogroups of transformations defined by linear PDE systems (Lie/Cartan pseudogroups); biholomorphic maps in several complex variables; quasi-/generalized conformal maps; Liouville rigidity
results.usually_credited_to: Lie and Cartan (infinite continuous groups/pseudogroups, 1880s-1900s); Poincare (1907, biholomorphic inequivalence of ball and bidisc); Liouville (1850, rigidity)

results.what: Parable: ideal theory as an 'express steamer' versus finitely many laborious constructive procedures
results.modern_name: Conceptual/abstract versus constructive-computational method (Hilbert's methodological stance, cf. finiteness theorem controversy with Gordan)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert's general methodological position is well known (Zahlbericht 1897; invariant theory 1888-93); this specific metaphor is not widely cited to my knowledge

deep.surprise_reason: Part (A) is a speculative research note with no result. The idea of generalizing conformal maps via composition-closed linear PDE systems is in the Lie-Cartan circle of ideas and is interesting as evidence of Hilbert's interests around 1894-95, but it is not a theorem. Part (B) is a vivid, apparently unpublished statement of Hilbert's well-known preference for conceptual over computational methods. It is quotable for historians but not mathematically new.

checkable.asserts: Real/imaginary parts of a holomorphic function of two complex variables satisfy the linear Cauchy-Riemann system in each variable (all four expressions are 0).

checkable.sympy: x1,y1,x2,y2=symbols('x1 y1 x2 y2',real=True); u=x1+I*y1; w=x2+I*y2; G=expand((u**2+w)**2*(u+w**2)); P=re(G); Q=im(G); simplify(diff(P,x1)-diff(Q,y1))
checkable.asserts: A composition of holomorphic maps (here f(u,w)=u^2+w, g(u,w)=u+w^2 inserted into a holomorphic polynomial) again satisfies the Cauchy-Riemann system, illustrating closure under composition (result is 0).

checkable.sympy: x,y,z=symbols('x y z',real=True); r2=x**2+y**2+z**2; X=Matrix([x,y,z])/r2; J=X.jacobian([x,y,z]); simplify(J.T*J - eye(3)/r2**2)
checkable.asserts: Inversion in the unit sphere of R^3 is conformal: J^T J = |x|^(-4) I (zero matrix). It is one of the Moebius maps to which Liouville's theorem restricts conformal maps in dimension 3, motivating the search for another class.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'lung durch' should be 'dung durch' (end of 'Abbil-dung' from the previous page).
Line 1: 'f_2(u,w_1)\, f_2'(u,w)' is better read as 'f(u,w), f'(u,w)'. The mark after the first w is a comma, not a subscript 1, and the letter before the bracket is a single function symbol.
Line 8: 'wie Hertz Mechanik' – the manuscript appears to have 'Herz Mechanik' (Hertz, Prinzipien der Mechanik).
Line 15: 'dass[?]' at the start of the line completes 'vorausge-setzt dass' ('vorausge-' is hyphenated across the line; the 'setzt' may be abbreviated or omitted).
Line 17: 'rascher u. sicher' – the manuscript may read 'sicherer'; uncertain.
The superscript insertion 'Billets auf den nächsten' above 'Schnelldampfers' is correctly identified as an interlinear addition.
